editorial.headline: Clay, Ceramic and Porcelain Products Beyond Building Materials
editorial.standfirst: A precise KBLI for makers of non-building clay, ceramic and porcelain goods, nationally open to foreign investment and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is for manufacturers working with clay, ceramic and porcelain outside the building-materials lane. Its scope is deliberately residual but still quite concrete: it catches products made from those materials that are not otherwise classified in the record, including ceramic furniture and other ceramic goods. In plain terms, this is not about tiles, bricks or construction inputs. It is for the workshop, factory or production house making other finished objects from clay, ceramics or porcelain, where the material defines the industrial activity.

That breadth matters because the code is open across every business scale named in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. A small ceramic studio and a larger industrial producer can both sit within the same activity description if the actual work is manufacturing these non-building products. The editorial point is not that every business will look alike, but that the classification is built around the production activity itself: making the goods, not simply trading them, displaying them or using them as part of another service.

Nationally, the investment picture is straightforward. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the maximum foreign ownership recorded is 100%. There is no foreign-share haircut in the slim record, so the national reading is clean: a foreign-owned company can use this activity code up to full foreign ownership, with the cited basis given as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Nothing in the record adds a minimum capital figure, special licence, production threshold or timetable, so none should be inferred. The reliable fact is the national openness, the 100% ceiling, and the availability across the listed scales.

Bali is often where the sharper question appears, because the province applies an island-wide, permanent moratorium blocking all Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA. Here, however, the Bali-side status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record says the OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, which means it is not blocked by that moratorium. The honest conclusion is therefore not a hidden restriction but a usable distinction: nationally open, 100% foreign-owned, and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the moratorium described in the record. For a founder, the discipline is to keep the classification tied to real manufacturing of non-building clay, ceramic or porcelain products, then read Bali through the recorded risk reason rather than assuming the moratorium catches everything.
